title: Intrinsic Dimensionality Explains the Effectiveness of Language Model Fine-Tuning
authors: Armen Aghajanyan, Sonal Gupta, Luke Zettlemoyer

findings.claim: Training 200 parameters through a fixed random projection gets RoBERTa to 90% of full fine-tuning on MRPC, and larger models have lower intrinsic dimension.
findings.quote: by optimizing only 200 trainable parameters randomly projected back into the full space, we can tune a RoBERTa model to achieve 90% of the full parameter performance levels on MRPC

quantities.condition: derived: 200 params * 32 bits; projection regenerated from a seed; RoBERTa-Large, 90% of full FT on MRPC
derived: same update tied to a 90%-of-FT capability

findings.bears_on: Classic evidence that a fine-tune can be described in KB, not GB, given the base model and a seed; U can be tiny.

findings.claim: Larger pretrained models need fewer intrinsic dimensions for the same task.
findings.quote: larger models tend to have lower intrinsic dimension

quantities.condition: RoBERTa-Large, MRPC (Table 1); QQP 774

findings.bears_on: Points to even smaller U at frontier scale (extrapolation).

findings.claim: Tuning 200 parameters randomly projected into RoBERTa's full space reaches 90% of full fine-tuning on MRPC.
findings.quote: by optimizing only 200 trainable parameters randomly projected back into the full space, we can tune a RoBERTa model to achieve 90% of the full parameter performance levels on MRPC.

quantities.condition: RoBERTa, MRPC, 90% of full FT
derived: 200 x 32-bit floats plus a seed

findings.bears_on: Fine-tuning a task to 90% needs only ~6e3 bits in a seeded subspace, the lower floor on seed-based U.

findings.claim: Larger pretrained models have lower intrinsic dimension for fine-tuning.
findings.quote: larger models tend to have lower intrinsic dimension after a fixed number of pre-training updates
findings.bears_on: Seed-based fine-tuning gets cheaper as N grows: U per task falls with scale.

title: Dion: Distributed Orthonormalized Updates
authors: Kwangjun Ahn, Byron Xu, Natalie Abreu, Ying Fan, Gagik Magakyan, Pratyusha Sharma et al.

findings.claim: Dion's low-rank orthonormalized updates (r = d/2 to d/16) approach full-rank Muon more closely as models grow from 354M to 3B.
findings.quote: Figure 2: Validation loss for Dion at three low-rank settings (r = d/2, d/4, d/16) versus full-rank Muon. Larger models are increasingly robust to low-rank update.

quantities.condition: smallest rank fraction r/d tested

findings.bears_on: The cost of rank-reduced updates shrinks with scale, so low-rank m_A rises toward 1.

title: LoRA-XS: Low-Rank Adaptation with Extremely Small Number of Parameters
authors: Klaudia Bałazy, Mohammadreza Banaei, Karl Aberer, Jacek Tabor

findings.claim: A small trainable r x r matrix between frozen SVD factors of the base weights cuts adapter storage over 100x versus LoRA at 7B.
findings.quote: This design enables LoRA-XS to reduce storage requirements by over 100x

quantities.condition: 7B models

findings.bears_on: Adapters built from the committed model's own SVD carry only r^2 numbers per matrix, pushing U for a frontier model into the sub-MB range.

findings.claim: A rank-16 LoRA-XS for GPT-3 costs about 96 KB per personalized model.
findings.quote: adapting GPT-3 with LoRA-XS (rank 16) for 1 million personalized models requires just 96GB of storage, compared to LoRA’s 144TB

quantities.condition: derived: 96 GB / 1e6 models; GPT-3 175B, rank 16 (storage calculation, not a trained 175B run)

findings.bears_on: At 175B an SVD-based adapter is ~0.1 MB, well under K; decoding needs the base SVD, which is a function of theta.

title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
authors: Dan Biderman, Jacob Portes, Jose Javier Gonzalez Ortiz, Mansheej Paul, Philip Greengard, Connor Jennings, et al.

findings.claim: Full fine-tuning learns perturbations of 10-100x higher rank than typical LoRA settings.
findings.quote: full finetuning learns perturbations with a rank that is 10-100$\times$ greater than typical LoRA configurations

quantities.condition: Llama-2-7B full FT: ~50% of singular vectors (~2000/4096) needed for 90% of variance (Section 6)

findings.bears_on: Unconstrained SFT on new domains has high update.rank (~half of full), so naturally trained deltas compress poorly by rank.

findings.claim: For math instruction tuning of Llama-2-7B, rank 64 nearly matches full fine-tuning (GSM8K 0.624 vs 0.642).
findings.quote: $r=64$ suffices to approach full finetuning and achieve GSM8K=0.624

quantities.condition: Llama-2-7B math IFT, all modules; full FT 0.642, r=256 0.634

findings.bears_on: Central update.rank for SFT-style instruction tuning is ~16-256; continued pretraining needs more.

findings.claim: For code and math with ~100K instruction pairs or ~20B tokens of continued pretraining, low-rank LoRA substantially underperforms full fine-tuning on Llama-2-7B.
findings.quote: In continued pretraining, the performance gap between full finetuning and LoRA is not closed even with high ranks.
findings.bears_on: Domain-scale new knowledge (billions of tokens) needs high-rank, high-U updates; the broad-improvement tier via new data does not fit in small adapters.

findings.claim: Full fine-tuning perturbations have rank 10-100x higher than typical LoRA configurations, and the rank grows during training.
findings.quote: The rank of the perturbation grows as training progresses, with ranks 10-100$\times$ higher than typical LoRA configurations (Figure 6).

quantities.condition: derived: 10-100x typical LoRA ranks (16-256 assumed); Llama-2-7B code/math full FT

findings.bears_on: Knowledge-acquiring updates have high b_w.delta; only elicitation-type updates are low rank.

title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
authors: Tim Dettmers, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, Luke Zettlemoyer

findings.claim: LoRA on a 4-bit base reaches 99.3% of ChatGPT on Vicuna with a 65B model after 24 hours on one GPU.
findings.quote: reaching 99.3% of the performance level of ChatGPT while only requiring 24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU
findings.bears_on: Strong chat instruction tuning is reachable with LoRA-sized updates, so SFT-style U ~10s-100s of MB is realistic.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities n/a

findings.claim: For 7B, typical LoRA weights equal to 0.2% of the model take 26 MB.
findings.quote: with LoRA weights equivalent to commonly used 0.2% of the original model weights [28, 37], the LoRA input gradients have a memory footprint of 567 MB while the LoRA parameters take up only 26 MB

quantities.condition: LLaMA 7B, LoRA = 0.2% of weights
derived: 26 MB * 8 / 7e9

findings.bears_on: Typical SFT LoRA at 7B is ~26 MB, above K; b_w.delta ~0.03 in this common setting.

findings.claim: A 9k-example dataset beat a 450k-example one for chatbot quality.
findings.quote: a 9k sample dataset (OASST1) outperformed a 450k sample dataset (FLAN v2, subsampled) on chatbot performance
findings.bears_on: Instruction-tuning information content is set by small curated data, consistent with small U.

title: Mixture-of-LoRAs: An Efficient Multitask Tuning for Large Language Models
authors: Wenfeng Feng, Chuzhan Hao, Yuewei Zhang, Yu Han, Hao Wang

findings.claim: Each LoRA expert and the single-LoRA baseline have 143M trainable parameters, so the full mixture of eight is about 1.15B parameters plus a 1.05M-parameter router.
findings.quote: | trainable parameters | 143M | 143M | 143M*8+1.05M |

quantities.condition: Qwen-7b base
derived: (143M x 8 + 1.05M) params x 16 bits, about 2.3 GB, roughly 200-900x K

findings.bears_on: Confirms the draft's 'baseline adapter the same size as an individual expert', but the mixture is 8x larger than the baseline, so its gain is not a free capability-per-bit gain and U is far above K.

findings.claim: The mixture lowers average perplexity from 4.0128 (single LoRA) and 3.9450 (mixed-data LoRA) to 3.7987 and raises Exam accuracy from 39.07% to 44.55%.

quantities.condition: derived: Exam accuracy 44.55% (MoA) minus 39.07% (Single-LoRA), Qwen-7b

findings.bears_on: Supports the draft's claim of improvement over a same-size single adapter; it moves capability.bits only weakly because the comparison is at 8x the update size.

title: Higher Layers Need More LoRA Experts
authors: Chongyang Gao, Kezhen Chen, Jinmeng Rao, Baochen Sun, Ruibo Liu, Daiyi Peng, et al.
venue: arXiv preprint (published as 'MoLA: MoE LoRA with Layer-wise Expert Allocation', Findings of NAACL 2025)

findings.claim: MoLA uses rank-8 LoRA experts with top-2 routing at each layer, on LLaMA2-7B, compared against a single rank-64 LoRA.
findings.quote: The rank of each LoRA expert is 8 and we adopt top-2 for the router.
findings.location: Section 4 (implementation details); baseline: 'Specifically, the rank of LoRA is 64.'

quantities.condition: LLaMA2-7B, top-2 routing per token per layer

quantities.unit: effective rank per token per layer
quantities.condition: derived: 2 active experts x rank 8

findings.bears_on: Matches the draft's description; each token sees an effective rank-16 update per layer while the total update is a mixture of many experts, so U is set by all experts, not by one.

findings.claim: Only MoLA-2468 beats the rank-64 LoRA baseline on all six benchmarks (by 0.35 to 3.44 points); the other variants trail LoRA on CoLA and two on RTE, so the quoted sentence overstates the paper's own Table 1.
findings.quote: MoLA variants outperform the LoRA baseline on all the benchmarks.

quantities.condition: derived: largest gain of MoLA-2468 over LoRA rank 64 (CSQA 78.95 vs 75.51), LLaMA2-7B; smallest gain 0.35 (MRPC)

findings.bears_on: Adapter mixtures give incremental gains at best (largest +5.8 for MoLA-8888 on OpenbookQA), so the draft's 'incrementally outperform' holds, but only for the best allocation.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim overstated, quantities derived-ok; corrected here: The quote is verbatim, but the paper's Table 1 contradicts it for most variants: only MoLA-2468 beats LoRA on all six tasks (by 0.35-3.44, matching the derived numbers), the other four variants fall below LoRA on CoLA (85.43-86.28 vs 86.29) and two also on RTE, and the largest variant gain is +5.8 (MoLA-8888 OpenbookQA 82.8 vs 77.0).

title: Scalable Parameter and Memory Efficient Pretraining for LLM: Recent Algorithmic Advances and Benchmarking
authors: Athanasios Glentis, Jiaxiang Li, Qiulin Shang, Andi Han, Ioannis Tsaknakis, Quan Wei et al.

findings.claim: With a proper optimizer and hyperparameters, full-rank training beats memory-efficient methods; high-rank updates are key for low-rank methods.
findings.quote: We observe that with a proper choice of optimizer and hyperparameters, full-rank training delivers the best performance, as expected. We also notice that incorporating high-rank updates in low-rank approaches is the key to improving their performance.
findings.bears_on: Low-rank methods have m_A at or below 1 against tuned full-rank training.

title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning with Diff Pruning
authors: Demi Guo, Alexander M. Rush, Yoon Kim

findings.claim: Learning a sparse diff with an L0 penalty matches full fine-tuning on GLUE while changing 0.5% of BERT's parameters.
findings.quote: Diff pruning can match the performance of finetuned baselines on the GLUE benchmark while only modifying 0.5% of the pretrained model’s parameters per task

quantities.condition: BERT-Large, GLUE

findings.bears_on: Low end of update.fraction_changed when sparsity is trained in.

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
authors: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, et al.

findings.claim: A rank-4 LoRA on query and value projections of GPT-3 175B shrinks the checkpoint from 350 GB to 35 MB.
findings.quote: With r=4 and only the query and value projection matrices being adapted, the checkpoint size is reduced by roughly 10,000× (from 350GB to 35MB)

quantities.condition: GPT-3 175B, r=4, Wq and Wv only, FP16
derived: 35 MB * 8 / 175e9
GPT-3 175B adaptation

findings.bears_on: A 175B fine-tune at matched quality fits in 35 MB, about 3-14x over K, in 16-bit and without further compression.

findings.claim: Rank 1 or 2 suffices for GPT-3 adaptation even though the full rank is 12,288.
findings.quote: a very low rank (i.e., r in Figure 1 can be one or two) suffices even when the full rank (i.e., d) is as high as 12,288

quantities.condition: GPT-3 175B, Wq and Wv, WikiSQL/MNLI

findings.bears_on: Sets the low end of update.rank at 1 for narrow fine-tunes.

title: Editing Models with Task Arithmetic
authors: Gabriel Ilharco, Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Mitchell Wortsman, Suchin Gururangan, Ludwig Schmidt, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, et al.

findings.claim: A fine-tune's weight delta (task vector) is a direction that can be added, negated and combined to steer the model.
findings.quote: A task vector specifies a direction in the weight space of a pre-trained model, such that movement in that direction improves performance on the task.
findings.bears_on: Frames an update as a separable object relative to committed theta, the premise behind b_w.delta and U.

findings.claim: Task vectors for different tasks are nearly orthogonal.
findings.quote: Task vectors are typically close to orthogonal.
findings.bears_on: Distinct updates share little structure, so U for multiple tasks adds roughly linearly.

title: DeltaDQ: Ultra-High Delta Compression for Fine-Tuned LLMs via Group-wise Dropout and Separate Quantization
authors: Yanfeng Jiang, Zelan Yang, Bohua Chen, Shen Li, Yong Li, Tao Li

findings.claim: Group-wise dropout plus separate quantization reaches 128x on WizardMath-7B and 512x on WizardMath-70B with acceptable loss.
findings.quote: achieving $128\times$ compression for the WizardMath-7B model and $512\times$ compression for the WizardMath-70B model

quantities.condition: derived: 16 bits / 512x; WizardMath-70B GSM8K 79.90 vs 81.80 original (Table 3)
derived: 16 bits / 128x; WizardMath-7B GSM8K 52.69 vs 55.49 original (Table 2)

findings.bears_on: The lowest measured post-hoc b_w.delta for a naturally trained SFT delta: ~0.03 bits/weight at 70B with ~98% of GSM8K kept.

findings.claim: At the same 512x ratio on 70B, DARE collapses to 37.45 and DeltaZip to 48.74 GSM8K, while DeltaDQ keeps 79.90.
findings.location: Table 3 (Accuracy comparison of WizardMath-70B under ultra-high compression ratio)

quantities.condition: derived: 16/512; DARE 37.45, DeltaZip 48.74 at the same ratio

findings.bears_on: Below ~0.1 bits/weight the result depends heavily on the code; generic sparsifiers fail there.

title: NOLA: Compressing LoRA using Linear Combination of Random Basis
authors: Soroush Abbasi Koohpayegani, K L Navaneet, Parsa Nooralinejad, Soheil Kolouri, Hamed Pirsiavash

findings.claim: Expressing LoRA factors as learned mixtures of seeded random bases makes a LLaMA-2 70B instruction tune about 20x smaller than rank-1 LoRA at equal accuracy.
findings.quote: on LLaMA-2 70B, our method is almost 20 times more compact than the most compressed LoRA without degradation in accuracy

quantities.condition: derived: 0.57M params * 2 bytes; LLaMA-2 70B (8-bit base), Alpaca instruction tuning, MMLU 69.4 vs LoRA 69.5 vs base 68.9 (Table 5)
derived: 0.57M * 16 / 70e9

findings.bears_on: A 70B instruction-tuning update fits in ~1 MB, under K, with seed-regenerated bases.

findings.claim: Rank-1 LoRA on all layers of LLaMA-2 needs 2.50M (7B), 3.91M (13B) and 12.94M (70B) parameters; NOLA needs 0.06M, 0.14M and 0.57M.
findings.quote: NOLA fine-tunes LLaMA-2 70B (8-bit) with $0.57M$ parameters, a $95\%$ reduction compared to rank-one LoRA.

quantities.condition: derived: rank-1 LoRA, 12.94M params * 2 bytes, LLaMA-2 70B

findings.bears_on: Even rank-1 LoRA on a dense 70B is ~26 MB (above K); getting under K needs sub-rank-1 parameterizations.

findings.claim: NOLA stores a LoRA as coefficients over seeded random bases plus the seed.
findings.quote: To reconstruct the model, we store the coefficients and the seed of the random generator which is a single scalar.
findings.bears_on: Seed-based encoding applies to backprop-trained adapters, so small U is not unique to ZO.

findings.claim: NOLA fine-tunes LLaMA-2 70B with 0.57M parameters, 95% fewer than rank-1 LoRA, at essentially equal MMLU.
findings.quote: NOLA fine-tunes LLaMA-2 70B (8-bit) with 0.57M parameters, a 95% reduction compared to rank-one LoRA

quantities.condition: derived: 0.57M coefficients x 16 bits; MMLU 69.4 vs LoRA 69.5

findings.bears_on: A 70B instruction fine-tune fits in ~9e6 bits as seeds plus coefficients, inside K.

title: VeRA: Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation
authors: Dawid J. Kopiczko, Tijmen Blankevoort, Yuki M. Asano

findings.claim: Training only scaling vectors on frozen random matrices matches LoRA's instruction tuning with 100x fewer parameters (Llama2-13B: 2.4M vs 250.3M; MT-Bench 5.93 vs 5.77).
findings.quote: We find that despite the 100x reduction in the number of trainable parameters, our method closely matches the performance of LoRA-based finetuning.

quantities.condition: derived: 2.4M params * 2 bytes; Llama2-13B instruction tuning, MT-Bench 5.93 vs LoRA 5.77
derived: 2.4M * 16 / 13e9

findings.bears_on: An instruction-tuning update for a 13B model fits within K (4.8 MB) using seed-regenerated random bases.

findings.claim: Frozen shared random low-rank matrices plus trained scaling vectors match LoRA with 10x fewer trainable parameters.
findings.quote: using a single pair of low-rank matrices shared across all layers and learning small scaling vectors instead

quantities.unit: x fewer trainable parameters than LoRA
quantities.condition: GLUE, RoBERTa-large; also instruction-tuned 7B and 13B

findings.bears_on: A backprop-trained update can also be a seed plus a small vector, lowering U with modest decode.

title: TT-LoRA MoE: Unifying Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
authors: Pradip Kunwar, Minh N. Vu, Maanak Gupta, Mahmoud Abdelsalam, Manish Bhattarai

findings.claim: A separately trained router picks exactly one tensor-train adapter per input, so the mixture behaves like a task classifier over a bank of tiny task adapters.
findings.quote: A sparse MoE router, trained separately, dynamically leverages base model representations to select exactly one specialized adapter per input at inference time
findings.bears_on: Supports the draft's 'single expert per input' wording, but because routing is per input over 17 classification tasks it says nothing about per-token capability bought by an update, so it does not move U for open-ended training.

findings.claim: The 'rank-5' adapter is a tensor-train decomposition with 33,920 total parameters on Llama-3.2-1B, against 1,703,936 for a rank-16 LoRA on the same layers.
findings.quote: it uses roughly 2% of the trainable parameters (33,920) compared to LoRA's 1,703,936 parameters for the same adaptation layer

quantities.condition: TT-rank 5 adapter on Q/V projections of Llama-3.2-1B
derived: 33,920 params x 16 bits = 542,720 bits (about 68 KB), roughly 1-3% of K

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: the draft calls it a 'rank-5 expert', but 5 is a tensor-train rank (33,920 parameters in total), not a LoRA of rank 5; an update this small fits well inside K, so it would push U far below K for narrow classification tasks.

findings.claim: On average across 17 classification tasks TT-LoRA scores 79.58 against 80.99 for rank-16 LoRA, with large drops on BoolQ and Winogrande, so it approaches rather than matches LoRA.
findings.location: Table 4 (LoRA vs TT-LoRA; BoolQ 77.81 vs 68.58, Winogrande_l 65.06 vs 54.73)

quantities.condition: derived: TT-LoRA average 79.58 minus LoRA average 80.99 over 17 classification tasks, Llama-3.2-1B

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: 'able to match the performance of a rank-16 adapter' overstates the result (1.4 points lower on average, up to 10 points lower on single tasks), so capability per bit of tiny adapters is somewhat lower than the draft implies.

findings.claim: The authors limit their claims to homogeneous classification settings and leave generation and question answering to future work.
findings.quote: uniform TT-shape, TT-rank, Alpha values, and task type (classification)
findings.bears_on: Confirms the draft's caveat that results cover only Llama-3.2-1B classification, so this source cannot set b_w.delta or U for generative fine-tuning.

title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
authors: Chunyuan Li, Heerad Farkhoor, Rosanne Liu, Jason Yosinski

findings.claim: Training in a random low-dimensional subspace bounds a solution's description length and compresses networks over 100x.
findings.quote: the method is a simple technique for constructively obtaining an upper bound on the minimum description length of a solution. A byproduct of this construction is a simple approach for compressing networks, in some cases by more than 100 times.

quantities.condition: random-subspace training of small networks (MNIST, CIFAR, RL tasks)

findings.bears_on: Gives the method behind seed-plus-coefficients updates, whose size upper-bounds U.

findings.claim: A network trained in a 750-dim random subspace is stored as two seeds plus 750 floats, 260x smaller.
findings.quote: the 750 floating point numbers in $\theta^{(d)}_{*}$. It leads to compression (assuming 32-bit floats) by a factor of 260$\times$ from 793kB to only 3.2kB, or 0.4% of the full parameter size.

quantities.condition: derived: 3.2 kB x 8; MNIST FC network

findings.bears_on: Random-subspace training gives the same seeds-plus-scalars structure as ZO, with U = subspace dimension x float width.

findings.claim: Intrinsic dimension measures task difficulty: Atari Pong from pixels is about as hard as CIFAR-10.
findings.quote: playing Atari Pong from pixels is about as hard as classifying CIFAR-10.
findings.bears_on: Gives a capability-per-scalar scale: harder tasks need more seeded directions.

findings.claim: Memorizing shuffled MNIST labels needs an intrinsic dimension of 190k, about 3.8 floats per random label.
findings.quote: it yields dint90 = 190k. We can interpret this as requiring 3.8 floats to memorize each random label (at 90% accuracy).

quantities.condition: shuffled-label MNIST, 50k images

findings.bears_on: Memorization (pretraining-like novel information) needs subspace dimension proportional to data, unlike fine-tuning.

title: Branch-Train-Merge: Embarrassingly Parallel Training of Expert Language Models
authors: Margaret Li, Suchin Gururangan, Tim Dettmers, Mike Lewis, Tim Althoff, Noah A. Smith et al.

findings.claim: Branch-Train-Merge over 64 domains gives a 22.4B-parameter LM equal to a Transformer trained with 2.5x the compute, with gains growing with domain count.
findings.quote: the resulting LM (22.4B total parameters) performs as well as a Transformer LM trained with 2.5 times more compute. These gains grow with the number of domains

quantities.condition: BTM vs Transformer LM, 64 domains, 192B tokens

findings.bears_on: Embarrassingly parallel experts with no synchronization: m_A about 2.5 in perplexity.

title: ExCP: Extreme LLM Checkpoint Compression via Weight-Momentum Joint Shrinking
authors: Wenshuo Li, Xinghao Chen, Han Shu, Yehui Tang, Yunhe Wang

findings.claim: Residuals between adjacent pretraining checkpoints (weights plus Adam momentum) compress ~70x on Pythia-410M and ~24x on PanGu-pi-7B, nearly losslessly.
findings.quote: we achieve approximately $70\times$ compression for the Pythia-410M model, with the final performance being as accurate as the original model on various downstream tasks

quantities.condition: derived: 0.06 GB * 8 / 410M, weights+optimizer state; Pythia-410M, avg 42.93 vs 43.11
derived: 4.10 GB * 8 / 7e9, weights+optimizer state; PanGu-pi-7B 98.59G -> 4.10G, avg 57.09 vs 56.71

findings.bears_on: Pretraining-style updates (with optimizer state) stay at ~1-5 bits/param, far above fine-tune deltas; b_w stays high for pretraining-like training.

title: BitDelta: Your Fine-Tune May Only Be Worth One Bit
authors: James Liu, Guangxuan Xiao, Kai Li, Jason D. Lee, Song Han, Tri Dao, et al.

findings.claim: A post-hoc sign-plus-scale quantization takes full fine-tune deltas (SFT, RLHF, RoPE scaling) to 1 bit per weight with small quality loss, up to 70B.
findings.quote: We introduce a simple post-fine-tuning method, BitDelta, which successfully quantizes this delta down to 1 bit without compromising performance.

quantities.condition: Llama-2, Mistral, MPT up to 70B; embeddings and LM head left uncompressed; scale distillation brings TruthfulQA/GSM8K within 1-2 points of the fine-tune

findings.bears_on: Sets a near-lossless ceiling of about 1 bit/weight for b_w.delta of naturally trained full fine-tunes, so b_w.delta <= 1 even without special training.

findings.claim: On Llama 2-70B the compressed delta is 8.95 GB against 137.95 GB for the full model (15.41x), i.e. about 1 bit per weight including the uncompressed embeddings.

quantities.condition: Llama 2-70B delta
derived: 8.95 GB * 8 / 70e9 weights

findings.bears_on: A naturally trained 70B fine-tune compressed this way is ~9 GB, about 1000x over K, so it needs sharding unless training is constrained.

findings.claim: Full-parameter fine-tune deltas are high rank, so low-rank SVD approximations of them do worse than 1-bit quantization.
findings.quote: Deltas from full parameter fine-tuning are fairly high rank, making low-rank approximations difficult.

quantities.condition: Llama 2-7B -> Vicuna-7B v1.5 delta, 4096x4096 matrix; qualitative: cumulative explained variance rises slowly

findings.bears_on: Naturally trained full-FT updates are not low rank, so update.rank is high unless the training itself is LoRA-constrained.

title: Kimi-K2-Instruct config.json
authors: Moonshot AI

findings.claim: Kimi K2 (~1T parameters) has 61 layers (1 dense), 384 routed experts plus 1 shared per MoE layer, hidden size 7168 and expert width 2048; from this, a rank-1 LoRA on every routed expert's three matrices is ~637M parameters.
findings.quote: "hidden_size": 7168, "initializer_range": 0.02, "intermediate_size": 18432, "kv_lora_rank": 512, "max_position_embeddings": 131072, "model_type": "kimi_k2", "moe_intermediate_size": 2048, "moe_layer_freq": 1, "n_group": 1, "n_routed_experts": 384

quantities.condition: derived: rank-1 LoRA on gate/up/down of all 384 routed experts x 60 MoE layers = 23,040 experts * 3 * (7168+2048) = 637M params * 2 bytes (bf16)
derived: same 637M params at 1 bit each
derived: 1.02e10 bits / 1.03e12 weights (routed experts only)
derived: rank-1 LoRA on all non-routed matrices (MLA attention 3.81M + shared experts 1.66M + dense MLP 0.08M = 5.55M params) in bf16
derived: LoRA-XS r=2 (4 params) on all ~69,600 linear modules = 278k params in bf16
derived: merging a rank-1 LoRA into all ~1.03e12 weights at ~2 flops/weight, about 30 tokens of forward pass at 32B active params

findings.bears_on: Answers the U question: a rank-1 adapter on every expert of a 1T MoE is ~1.3 GB (115-510x over K), but SVD-based or tied adapters fit under K and decode cheaply.

title: Learning to Reason in 13 Parameters
authors: John X. Morris, Niloofar Mireshghallah, Mark Ibrahim, Saeed Mahloujifar
